Text: A {{c1::nested class}} is any class defined within the body of another enclosing class.
Extra: Nested classes are divided into two main categories: static nested classes and inner classes (non-static).

Text: A {{c1::static nested class}} behaves like a top-level class that has been nested inside another class, and does not have an implicit reference to an instance of the outer class.
Extra: It can access static members of the outer class directly (even private ones), but not instance members.

Text: An {{c1::inner class}} is a non-static nested class, meaning every instance of it is implicitly bound to a specific instance of the outer class.
Extra: It maintains a hidden reference to the outer instance via OuterClassName.this.

Text: A {{c1::local inner class}} is defined within a block of code, typically inside a method body, and its scope is restricted to that block.
Extra: It cannot have access modifiers (public, private, protected) or be declared static.

Text: An {{c1::anonymous inner class}} is a local class without a name that is declared and instantiated at the same time using the new operator.
Extra: It must either extend an existing class or implement an interface, and cannot define a constructor.

Text: Local or anonymous inner classes can only access local variables and parameters from their enclosing method if they are {{c1::final or effectively final::what restriction?}}.
Extra: Effectively final means the variable's value is never modified after it is initialized.

Text: Prior to Java {{c1::16}}, inner classes (including local and anonymous classes) were not allowed to declare static members unless they were compile-time constants (static final).
Extra: Java 16 lifted this restriction, allowing static variables and methods inside inner classes.

Text: Inside an anonymous class, the "this" keyword refers to {{c1::the anonymous class instance itself}}, whereas inside a lambda expression, "this" refers to {{c2::the enclosing outer class instance}}.
Extra: This is because lambdas use lexical scoping rather than introducing a new scope level.

Text: At the bytecode level, private access between an outer class and its inner class is facilitated by compiler-generated static helper methods called {{c1::synthetic accessor methods}} (e.g., {{c2::access$000}}).
Extra: Since the JVM does not natively understand nested classes and treats them as separate class files (Outer.class and Outer$Inner.class), the compiler generates these package-private bridge methods to allow access to private members across class boundaries.
